title: E46 - AI for Judges? AAA CEO Bridget McCormack and Learned Hand CEO Shlomo Klapper
author: Bridget McCormack · Shlomo Klapper

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Court responsibility: AI requires lifecycle supervision
st.an: The source shifts the priority from lifecycle supervision and retained human judicial authority to court-capacity constraints. It presents AI as potentially supplying decision-making capacity that human staffing cannot provide and questions whether adjudication inherently requires a human component, without substantively addressing the cluster’s verification, confidentiality, security or institutional-governance safeguards.
qs: An AI could step in to give these judges the capacity they need to actually do their jobs and for the courts to actually function.

st.t: Human oversight: Accountability is not effective control
st.an: The source shifts the debate from making human oversight effective to overcoming court-capacity constraints through AI decision-making. It acknowledges anxiety about moving from copilot to agentic authority but questions whether adjudication inherently requires a human component, without addressing the cluster’s requirements for independent verification, intervention capacity, or expertise preservation.
qs: But in 2026, we're talking about AI acting as an agent, making decisions, taking actions.
An AI could step in to give these judges the capacity they need to actually do their jobs and for the courts to actually function.

st.t: Justice access: Direct AI use shifts risk downward
st.an: The source shifts the focus from direct-to-consumer assistance and downward risk transfer to court overload and AI-supported or AI-led adjudication. It presents judicial capacity as the central problem and questions whether human decision-making is indispensable, without substantively addressing users’ limited verification capacity, weak remedies or inequality risks.
qs: An AI could step in to give these judges the capacity they need to actually do their jobs and for the courts to actually function.

st.t: Machine judging: Accuracy cannot establish legitimate authority
st.an: The source shifts the debate from whether technical performance can confer legitimate judicial authority to courts’ urgent need for additional capacity and the claimed impartiality of “blind” justice. Although it recognises that moving AI from copilot to decision-maker creates anxiety, it questions rather than develops the cluster’s emphasis on consent, challenge rights, legal development and institutional authority.
qs: And that shift from co-pilot to decision-maker explains a lot of the friction we're seeing between how we view lawyers using AI versus how we might view judges.
An AI could step in to give these judges the capacity they need to actually do their jobs and for the courts to actually function.

st.t: Vendor value: Concentration forecasts face diverse competition
st.an: The source does not assess which legal-AI vendors will capture durable value or whether the market will concentrate. It redirects attention from vendor competition and returns to adoption, misuse, and unequal acceptance of AI use by lawyers versus adjudicators.
qs: So according to multiple surveys from Wharton, Law 360, Thomson Reuters and the ACC, a bunch, AI usage in the legal profession flipped from a minority to a clear majority.
Nearly 90% of lawyers were deeply supportive of AI in their own research and analytics, but that support drops to 23% when it comes to either a judge or an arbitrator using AI to make a decision.

st.t: Court AI: Existing failures set the comparison
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s central comparison with existing justice failures and unmet need, then materially extends it with a purpose-built judicial-support model intended to expand attention per case. Its time-saving claims and litigation-growth forecast remain anecdotal or predictive rather than evidence of improved accuracy, fairness or access outcomes.

So essentially what we've built is that, I didn't say my, the sort of the punchline is, is that Learned Hand is essentially the tool that if I was still a clerk, I would have been able to give the same attention to every case as I gave to that first case.

st.t: Production model: Institutional absorption governs AI value
st.an: The source accepts that AI value depends on selective, institutionally appropriate deployment with human oversight, then materially extends the cluster into adjudication and private dispute resolution. It distinguishes suitability by professional role and proposes a bounded workflow in which LLMs generate equitable options while humans remain important for judgment and ongoing relationships; its adoption and speed claims remain experiential predictions rather than measured outcomes.

st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s service-redesign framing and extends it to judicial work: adoption should begin with judges’ case-specific truth-finding needs rather than generic AI capability, using purpose-built systems and infrastructure. Its reported uptake and expected acceptance remain product claims and predictions, not measured transformation effects.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts selective, human-led deployment and materially extends it to adjudication. It distinguishes AI-suitable information-processing from moral or coercive decisions that must remain human, while proposing purpose-built, transparent systems and dispute-specific pathways rather than general automation.

st.t: Agentic workflows: Tacit expertise resists easy transfer
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s qualified copilot framing: AI may expand creative legal problem-solving, including equitable options, while human involvement remains important where judgment and continuing relationships matter. st.t: Conditional optimism: User problems outrank AI branding
st.an: The source aligns with conditional optimism: it treats AI adoption as difficult to avoid, emphasizes building systems well enough to earn trust, and anticipates movement beyond the copilot role. However, these are predictions and recommendations rather than evidence that autonomous decision-making is reliable or transformative.
qs: So let's build it well so that we can grow trust.

st.t: Dispute resolution: Assistance differs from machine adjudication
st.an: Abramowitz supports the cluster’s legitimacy framing by questioning an idealised human-adjudicator baseline while acknowledging visible AI failures. He also distinguishes judicial decision support from AI arbitration, but provides no comparative performance evidence or deployment results establishing that machine adjudication is reliable or equivalent to human-reviewed assistance.
qs: Like we've seen fake cases submitted to judges, we've seen judges citing fake cases, we've seen AI avatars trying to argue motions and lawyers repeatedly getting sanctioned.
Plus, let's be clear, human judges make plenty of mistakes.

st.t: Justice capacity: AI potential requires deliberate implementation
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s emphasis on deliberate implementation by treating AI’s advance as unavoidable while urging trustworthy development rather than passive adoption. Its forecast that AI may move beyond a copilot role broadens the anticipated role of the technology, but remains speculative and supplies no evidence of improved access-to-justice outcomes.
qs: So let's build it well so that we can grow trust.
And I think this is a really, really critical conversation, something we're going to be following moving forward, as AI becomes a little bit more of a decision maker, not just a co-pilot.

st.t: Practitioner engagement: Redesign should precede technological certainty
st.an: The source supports engaging with and testing judicial AI before technological certainty, arguing that assessment should compare AI with fallible human judging and unavailable legal help rather than an error-free ideal. It also foregrounds access to dispute resolution, while acknowledging AI failures and not claiming proven improvements in judicial outcomes.

st.an: The source supports the cluster’s workflow-based account of trust by treating human oversight as part of governance and by suggesting that acceptance will grow when users observe practical service benefits. kp.k: Judicial AI faces distinct professional and regulatory resistance
kp.d: Host Zach Abramowitz frames acceptance of lawyers' AI use alongside resistance to judicial AI as a double standard. He reports nearly 90% support for lawyers' research and analytics but 23% for judicial or arbitral decision-making in a White & Case/Queen Mary survey; no sample or methodology is provided. He also reports that EU AI Act Annex 3 classifies administration-of-justice and alternative-dispute-resolution AI as high-risk. These are the host's reported findings and regulatory framing, rather than independently established conclusions in the episode.
qs: Nearly 90% of lawyers were deeply supportive of AI in their own research and analytics, but that support drops to 23% when it comes to either a judge or an arbitrator using AI to make a decision.
Annex 3 explicitly classifies AI used in the administration of justice or in alternative dispute resolution as high-risk.

kp.k: State courts lack capacity for sustained individual case attention
kp.d: Klapper and McCormack identify state courts as the principal target for capacity-building: they say 99% of cases occur there, with substantially fewer resources than federal courts. Klapper recounts a Texas judge disposing of 2,500 cases in a year, including hearings, which he interprets as half an hour per case; this is a particular judge's reported workload, not a documented population estimate. McCormack argues that five decades of incremental efforts have failed to meet public needs and that additional lawyers alone cannot solve the problem.
qs: I was just speaking to a judge in Texas who had disposed of 2,500 cases in a year.
Ninety-nine percent of cases are in state court.
And the resources are significantly less.
Because we're not going to lawyer our way out of the problem.

kp.k: Time scarcity can materially affect judicial outcomes
kp.d: Klapper recounts spending an entire week on his first appellate clerkship case, involving a 26-year-old sentenced to 30 years in prison, and attributes a 10-year sentence reduction to his examination of the record and inconsistencies. He argues that the same attention would have been impossible later in the term. This personal anecdote motivates Learned Hand's capacity proposition; his claim about what would have happened later is a counterfactual, not measured evidence.
qs: So I spent an entire week reading the record, understanding the case law, going through this massive amount of papers, finding many inconsistencies.
Based on my work, her sentence was reduced by 10 years.
The sad fact is that if she would have come towards the end of the term, she would have been serving out this extra 10 years.

kp.k: Learned Hand targets research, analysis and drafting for judges
kp.d: Klapper describes Learned Hand as judicial decision support, analogous to an AI law clerk, intended to extend judges' capacity rather than replace their authority. He relays a chief trial judge's feedback that a summary-judgment motion normally taking four hours took 10 minutes, and a civil-immunity motion normally taking three hours took five minutes. These are vendor-carried customer reports without disclosed evaluation methods, sample sizes or accuracy measurements.
qs: It's essentially close to an AI law clerk that can do research analysis and drafting.
Summary judgment motion, normally would have taken four hours, took 10 minutes.
It would normally would have taken three hours to take five minutes.
Our goal is very straightforward. It's to give the best tools to human judges and to get that.

kp.k: Lower litigation barriers could intensify court congestion
kp.d: Both guests predict that AI will lower the cost of bringing claims, enabling people with valid but previously unheard claims to enter court while worsening existing capacity constraints. Klapper cites an unspecified 92% unmet-needs figure and predicts '10, 12 X' litigation growth, without a timeframe or supporting model. His traffic and pandemic queueing analogies explain why even 20% or 40% docket growth could overwhelm courts already at capacity; the magnitude of future litigation is speculative.
qs: The barrier to entry is going to go to almost zero to get into court, which I honestly think is a good thing.
And an awful lot of people who have valid claims that have no way to have them heard.
there's 92 percent of cases, they say, are unmet needs.
So there's going to be like literally 10, 12 X the amount of litigation.

kp.k: Assess judicial AI against actual human performance
kp.d: McCormack argues that AI should be compared with imperfect, resource-constrained human adjudication, not an ideal of flawless decisions. She explicitly labels her story about a judge misidentifying her as anecdotal. Klapper points to appellate review as institutional recognition of human error and claims about 20% of cases are overturned, without identifying the denominator, jurisdiction or period; McCormack says rates are higher in some places. Their colloquial references to human 'hallucination' concern human mistakes, not measured generative-model fabrication rates.
qs: what are we measuring against?
I mean, it's not that useful for the larger conversation because it's an anecdote, but it's a reminder that as opposed to what should be the question.
The entire court system is predicated on the fact that judges make mistakes.
About 20 percent of cases are overturned.
Yet we expect technology to be perfect.

kp.k: AI should expand dispute-resolution choices rather than mandate substitution
kp.d: McCormack explicitly rejects routing every case to AI. She advocates additional judicial workflows and private dispute-resolution options, presenting AI arbitration as a further innovation following arbitration's historical emergence as an alternative to litigation. She suggests public preferences may differ from lawyers' preferences because many people cannot afford legal help, but presents this as a hypothetical polling proposition rather than a survey result.
qs: Just to be clear, my argument wasn't every case goes to AI. It was we can have more options now.
We have more options for how judges can resolve disputes, for workflows, for the kinds of things that Shlomo is building, for parties that want to resolve them without going to court.
We can give people a little bit more agency over their own disputes and let them resolve them in a binding process outside of court.

kp.k: Dispute characteristics determine the value of human involvement
kp.d: McCormack proposes a dispute-portfolio approach. She reports conversations with in-house teams about repetitive, document-governed supplier disputes that may involve substantial sums but little perceived need for human intervention. Conversely, family and small-business disputes involving continuing relationships may benefit more from human facilitation than speed or efficiency. Her argument separates enterprise dispute efficiency from access-to-justice benefits and does not use monetary value alone to determine suitability for automation.
qs: So this is why I think you need to think about a dispute portfolio.
I talked to in-house teams that have, you know, repetitive supplier disputes.
they know they're governed by documents, they're repetitive. They don't need a human in there.

A lot of small business disputes or family disputes where an actual human in the middle of that dispute, helping them get through that dispute and preserve a relationship, might matter more than the speed or efficiency that some technology could bring.

kp.k: Moral agency limits delegation of coercive judicial decisions
kp.d: Klapper distinguishes epistemic tasks—finding and processing information—from constitutive tasks involving political judgment and the legitimate exercise of state power. He argues that humans must retain decisions requiring moral agency, even as models improve. McCormack agrees and says disputes involving government should remain in public courtrooms before judges, whereas private parties should have more choice. Klapper specifically rejects AI imposing sentences while supporting assistive use in sentencing-related decisions.
qs: Those are fancy terms between finding information and crunching information and actually making a political decision.
AI agents are not moral agents.

So for things that require moral agency, which is a lot of what- That's what I was kind of the constitutive piece, is that that is where we're just like, that's not something we want to delegate to an AI.
should be done in public courtrooms by judges.
I don't think it should do the sentencing. I think that's dystopian. But I think there is a role for it as a tool and an assistive aid

kp.k: AI can generate equitable options without replacing human mediation
kp.d: McCormack questions a simple division under which legal rules suit AI while equity necessarily requires humans. She argues that language models can rapidly generate numerous creative settlement possibilities, potentially identifying an option acceptable to both sides that a human would take much longer to discover. This is a capability argument illustrated with a hypothetical list of 100 solutions, not a reported comparative study; she continues to emphasize human value in preserving relationships.
qs: Turns out large language models, as you know, are incredibly creative.
And they can think of like equitable options that a human might take weeks to think of.
number 78 might appeal to both parties in a way that it would have taken the human forever to find.
So I think everybody thinks like if it's equity, we need humans, if it's law, maybe we can be more comfortable. I'm not sure, I think it's more complicated and more nuanced.

kp.k: Emotional understanding remains a contested limitation
kp.d: Abramowitz speculates that AI lacks an emotional dimension necessary for some forms of comprehension and decision-making. McCormack broadly agrees that a missing piece exists, while noting iterative prompting and additional information can help. Klapper cautions against assuming this limitation will persist, citing his personal experience using Gemini as a presentation coach, and treats lack of moral agency as the more fundamental boundary. The discussion does not establish a tested technical limitation or future capability trajectory.
qs: But the one vector that hasn't necessarily been coded into AI, as far as I can tell, is emotion.
Although, as you know, you can go back and forth with it a lot and give it more information and ask it to try again.
I wouldn't bet up against the foundation models.
It really does understand nuances.

kp.k: Speakers report bias tests but disclose limited study details
kp.d: Klapper reports that a partner court tested Learned Hand by changing race, ethnicity and gender in otherwise identical cases and found no difference in outputs. McCormack says AAA is undertaking the same testing with its AI arbitrator and responds 'Same thing.' Neither supplies sample sizes, case selection, outcome measures or a published protocol. They argue that AI systems can be measured, audited and adjusted more readily than human bias; the episode's reported test result does not itself establish comprehensive absence of bias.
qs: So, they did a bias study with Learned Hand and they said, take the same cases and swap it out, and will there be any difference? There was no difference.
We're doing that with our AI arbitrator as well. Same thing.
It's a lot easier to de-bias the dataset than it is to de-bias the human.
You can measure it, and then you can audit it.

kp.k: Transparent assistive tools may challenge human preconceptions
kp.d: Klapper contrasts process-driven, transparent judicial assistance with the recidivism-prediction tool referred to as 'Compass' in the transcript. He recounts initially dismissing an airline's challenge to airport construction because of his defense-side bias, then reconsidering after Learned Hand identified a plausible case. The example illustrates his proposed human–AI complementarity mechanism, but is a personal anecdote rather than evidence of improved adjudicative outcomes.
qs: Again, this is different from Compass, which is a pre-sentencing tool trying to predict recidivism, which is a black box of things.
If you build it in a process-driven way, in a white box, clear box, open way, you can do this.
And it said, well, actually, there's a really possible case here.
and it helped me get through it, because I'm reading it with this tilt of, man, I can't believe I have another case, like this case to go through.

kp.k: Judges require tools distinct from advocacy-oriented AI
kp.d: Klapper argues that judicial work requires case-specific, truth-seeking support rather than generic legal memoranda, creative advocacy or agreement with the user's position. He reports judges finding those features unhelpful in tools offered to them and positions Learned Hand as purpose-built for adjudication. His description of lawyers as bending truth is his argumentative characterization, not an established statement of professional duties; his product differentiation and adoption claims are vendor assertions.
qs: It's either trying to give me a memo about the law in general, but I need to know about my case.
Or it's trying to be too creative and say, well, here's all these ideas and ways you can do it.
you can have two different windows and have two opposite ideas and it will both say, great, that's a great idea.
And what we've built at Learned Hand is something that is built for finding truth.
judges require a purpose-built AI.

kp.k: Trustworthy infrastructure and demonstrated utility underpin anticipated adoption
kp.d: The guests identify public confidence as central to judicial legitimacy and predict that direct experience of useful tools will increase acceptance. McCormack urges building systems well before acceptance becomes widespread, arguing that the profession cannot sit out this technological transition. Abramowitz describes AAA's AI arbitrator as combining transparency with a human in the loop, but the episode does not detail that governance arrangement. These are adoption expectations and design recommendations, not demonstrated adoption effects.
qs: It's all public confidence in what they do.
once they have an opportunity to see what technology can do for the service they provide, I think the floodgates open. That's my view.
But you also have human in the loop as part of that governance and trust structure
I don't think the legal profession gets to sit this particular change out.
So let's build it well so that we can grow trust.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The interviewees present AI as a way to expand judicial capacity, lower barriers to litigation, diversify dispute-resolution options and assist with bias reduction, while preserving human responsibility for certain decisions.
pts.d: Shlomo Klapper describes Learned Hand as judicial decision support for research, analysis and drafting, rather than a replacement judge. He claims it can enable attention to cases that staffing and time constraints currently prevent. He reports substantial time savings from a trial-court user's feedback. Klapper predicts dramatically cheaper litigation and potentially 10–12 times as much litigation, exacerbating court overload. Bridget McCormack similarly predicts near-zero barriers to entering court and greater access for people with valid but presently unheard claims. These are prospective claims, not reported measurements of increased filings. McCormack advocates additional AI-enabled options within courts and private dispute resolution, explicitly not sending every case to AI. She suggests repetitive, document-governed supplier disputes may not need human participation, while preserving relationships in family and small-business disputes may make a human intermediary especially valuable. She also claims language models can rapidly generate creative equitable solutions. Klapper distinguishes information-processing tasks from decisions exercising political or moral authority: AI should assist judges, including in sentencing, but should not itself impose sentences or take over decisions requiring moral agency. McCormack agrees that disputes involving government should remain before judges in public courts, while private parties should have more choices. Both describe AI as potentially easier to audit and de-bias than humans. Klapper claims purpose-built judicial AI is necessary because advocacy-oriented or general-purpose tools can be too creative, sycophantic or insufficiently case-specific. McCormack predicts that demonstrations of useful technology will unlock judicial adoption and argues that the profession cannot sit out this technological change.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The offered support consists chiefly of professional experience, product-user feedback, an internally described partner-court bias study, conversations with potential users and analogies; the transcript does not supply detailed study methods or a forecasting model.
pts.d: For judicial capacity, Klapper recounts spending a week reviewing a criminal appeal early in his clerkship, finding inconsistencies and contributing to a ten-year sentence reduction. He uses this human-work example to explain the attention he wants AI to make available across cases; it is not evidence of an AI-produced sentence reduction. He separately reports a chief trial judge's feedback that a summary-judgment task fell from four hours to ten minutes and a civil-immunity motion from three hours to five minutes. No independent timing study, sample size or accompanying quality assessment is supplied. His court-capacity account includes a conversation with a Texas judge who disposed of 2,500 cases in a year, including hearings, and claims about limited clerk support. McCormack supports the state-court focus through her judicial leadership experience. Klapper's litigation-growth prediction invokes unmet legal need, an asserted difficulty obtaining counsel for claims below $250,000 and a queuing-system analogy; no calculation establishing a 10–12-fold increase is presented. His reference to 92% unmet needs has no identified study or defined population in the transcript. For bias reduction, Klapper describes a partner-court study that changed race, ethnicity and gender in otherwise identical cases and found no difference in Learned Hand's results. McCormack says AAA is doing the same with its AI arbitrator and reports the same result. Neither provides sample sizes, metrics or a published protocol. Klapper also recounts Learned Hand prompting him to reconsider an initially dismissive view of an airline's claim. McCormack grounds the dispute-portfolio argument in conversations with in-house teams and illustrates creative equitable solutions through an example of generating 100 options. For the comparison with human judging, she invokes ten years reviewing judicial decisions and explicitly labels her mistaken-identity story anecdotal. Klapper invokes appellate correction and an approximately 20% overturning figure without specifying a jurisdiction, period or denominator. Their adoption expectations draw on contact with judges and reported uptake, not a quantified adoption study. Both speak as leaders of organisations developing the tools being discussed.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Existing product experiences are distinguished from near-term but undated forecasts; appropriate use depends on the dispute, human responsibility, system design and trust.
pts.d: At the time of the 2026 interview, Klapper presents Learned Hand's user feedback, partner-court bias testing and judicial uptake as existing experiences. McCormack describes parallel bias work with AAA's AI arbitrator as ongoing. The interviewees expect easier court access and increased litigation soon, but specify no date or period for the predicted 10–12-fold increase. McCormack's broader adoption forecast is conditional on judges seeing improvements in the service they provide; Klapper expects experience with additional options to change trust over time. He raises future voluntary selection of automated options in certain court cases as a possibility, not a current general arrangement. The principal present court model is augmentation: human judges use better tools. Klapper explicitly rejects replacing all humans with bots and distinguishes support for sentencing from AI doing the sentencing. His boundary is moral agency, not merely a temporary shortfall in model capability. McCormack's boundary includes government-related cases remaining in public courts and a continuing role for humans where parties must preserve relationships. The possibility of reducing human involvement in repetitive supplier disputes is therefore not a universal prediction of automated adjudication. She also cautions that the law/equity distinction alone does not settle suitability, because AI may help generate equitable options. Klapper conditions his bias-reduction claim on a process-driven, transparent approach, distinguished from a black-box recidivism predictor. McCormack stresses building systems well to grow trust.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The central beneficiaries and pressure points are under-resourced state courts, people with unmet legal needs, private disputants and corporate legal departments, with different proposed human roles across dispute types.
pts.d: Klapper and McCormack identify state trial courts as the highest-impact setting because of heavy caseloads and scarce support. Judges and clerks would gain research, record-analysis and drafting capacity; courts would simultaneously face increased demand if AI makes bringing claims easier. Individuals unable to obtain legal help could gain access to adjudication, though the interviewees predict that this would compound backlogs without additional capacity. Criminal defendants are implicated by Klapper's account of inadequate review time and by his proposal for assistance, but not automated sentencing. Private parties could choose additional forms of dispute resolution outside courts through providers such as AAA. Corporate in-house teams with repetitive supplier disputes are identified as potential users of more automated document-based resolution; these are buyer-side efficiency claims, distinct from the access-to-justice claims about unheard legal needs. Small businesses and families with ongoing relationships may benefit more from human facilitation, potentially supported by AI-generated settlement options. People in disputes with government are a category McCormack says should retain public adjudication by judges. Lawyers and the broader profession face pressure to adapt, while judicial tool developers must address the difference between advocacy and neutral adjudication. The transcript does not offer concrete predictions about law-firm staffing, billing structures or lawyer job losses.
